speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subsubtopic: PROTEST AGAINST REMOVAL OF SUBSIDY ON POWDERED SKIM MILK-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the statement by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) at the Food Conference that there is a nutrition crisis in Canada, in view of the fact that prices in Canada have risen by 15 per cent in the past year, and in view of the fact that low income earners already hit by food price inflation will have to pay approximately 34 cents more per pound for powdered skim milk as a result of the removal of the consumer subsidy by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and, further, that this will adversely affect already declining farm incomes, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise):
That in the opinion of this House the government should not remove the consumer subsidy on powdered skim milk.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has dropped the consumer subsidy for skim milk powder from his estimates, without warning or explanation. That this House directs the Minister of Agriculture to revise his estimates to include the consumer skim milk powder subsidy or other measures to subsidize milk for low income families in this country.

subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF RRAP ASSISTANCE-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under Standing Order 43. In view of the fact that, despite repeated promises to assist transients and other low income individuals living in slum housing conditions in areas such as the downtown east side of Vancouver, and in view of the fact that the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) specifically promised legislation during the 1977-78 fiscal year now rapidly coming to a close, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez):
That this House instruct the government to immediately introduce amendments to the National Housing Act, extending eligibility for assistance under the residential rehabilitation assistance program to the owners of hotels and rooming houses serving low income tenants, and that such assistance be available up to a ceiling amount of $4,000 per room, with provision for forgiveness clauses in loans offered under the program.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to present a motion on an important matter.
Considering the lack of sufficient measures which would improve on the present economic climate; considering that subsidies granted for research will never provide for an industrial strategy essential to permanent job creation; considering finally that recommendations contained in the brief of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association are part of the solution to the problems we are faced with, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey):

subsubtopic: PROVINCES REQUESTED TO UNDERTAKE EDUCATIONAL REFORM-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the terms of Standing Order 43, I request the unanimous consent of the House to present a motion related to an important issue.
February 23, 1978

As on this very day the provincial premiers are meeting in Montreal to reach an agreement on important and urgent reforms in the field of education for the minority groups of the official languages; recognizing that education is, under the Constitution, a matter of provincial jurisdiction; and considering the strong current of national interest in the matter, and the fact that millions of Canadians are now living in the expectancy of a solution that will contribute to their cultural and social survival, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Madawaska-Victoria (Mr. Corbin):
That this House send to the provincial premiers in meeeting a message indicating that we are at one with the objectives of equal linguistic rights in matters of education, and that the House of Commons supports them in their search for a genuine reform recognizing that all Canadians, in every province, have the right to be educated in the official language of their choice.

subsubtopic: WILLIAM IRVING-NICKEL MINER FATALLY INJURED AT WORK-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to ask for the unanimous consent of the House to deal with a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the fact that last Thursday Mr. William Irving, a miner with 31 years experience with Inco, was killed while working in a double-slicing operation at Frood Mine in Sudbury, that Mr. Irving and his fellow co-workers had vigorously protested what they considered to be a highly dangerous environment, that their immediate supervisor ordered them to continue to work under threat of job loss, that Mr. Irving leaves a widow and five children, and that this House congratulates beauty queens and expresses sympathy for the families of policemen unfortunately killed in fulfilling their duties, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn):
That this House extend its sympathy to the Irving family.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION ON RESERVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance who indicated
Oral Questions
in the debate last night that he felt there was no crisis with respect to our dollar. Our reserves have been falling very dramatically in recent weeks. Based on OECD figures for last November, which pointed out the Canadian foreign exchange reserves, relatively free reserves, were $1.6 billion at that time, compared to $16 billion in the case of the United Kingdom, almost $7 billion in the case of Italy, and even Ireland had more in foreign exchange free reserves according to OECD, would the Minister of Finance indicate if he does not feel at this point that our reserves are unduly precarious in their size?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the reserves of the Canadian government are published on the second working day of the month, and they are satisfactory just now. ALLEGED SURVEILLANCE OF MPs BY RCMP

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. Following a series of articles culminating on August 12 with an article in the Globe and Mail which contained allegations about the RCMP keeping files on members of parliament, as well as allegations about surveillance of members of parliament and others, 1 wrote the then solicitor general on August 12-
I can't hear.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby.

Mr. Speaker, I understand that because of the noise the Prime Minister did not hear my question. I will repeat it. On August 12, I wrote the then solicitor general concerning a series of allegations which were made in articles which had been published during that week in the Globe and Mail pertaining to the surveillance of members of parliament and the keeping of files on members of parliament by the RCMP. I did not receive a letter from the then solicitor general for some time. 1 subsequently wrote to the Prime Minister. I received a letter from the then solicitor general two days later which concluded with the following quotation of the then commissioner of the RCMP pertaining to allegations about surveillance:
I categorically deny that the RCMP has ever used electronic surveillance, including telephone taps or bugging devices in any form, anywhere, at any time against members of parliament, since the conviction of Fred Rose for espionage in 1947.
Following the submission of a petition by the hon. member for Central Nova yesterday which does contain information which, if it turns out to be true, is a serious contradiction of
February 23, 1978

that assertion, has the Prime Minister checked with the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs concerning the allegation made that he, in fact, had been the subject of electronic surveillance and that he, in fact, had been told about it later on?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following a question along those lines yesterday, I did ask the Solicitor General to inquire into the matter. We agreed from the outset that such a serious allegation should be referred to the McDonald commission. I understand that Commissioner McDonald has indicated that he is seized of the matter.
As far as we are concerned, I wrote a letter to the Leader of the Opposition giving the same kind of assurance with regard to security matters as I believe was read by the leader of the New Democratic Party. I have checked today to make sure that the information supplied to me for the purpose of this letter was supplied by our security officials, and the answer is yes, so there is an apparent contradiction between the advice 1 received and the allegations contained in this affidavit. We are not in a position yet to indicate how this contradiction can be resolved. Of course, I have confidence in my advisers and in the RCMP, rather than in a third party who is making these allegations.
For greater security, however, the Solicitor General is having an inquiry made within the RCMP to ascertain if there is any substance to the allegations.

Mr. Speaker, I can understand and accept part of the Prime Minister's answer when he says that the information was provided to him which formed the substance of his letter to the Leader of the Opposition, and the information that was provided to me, is being checked out: I fully accept that part of the answer.
My more specific question pertains to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. It seems to me the answer to that question should not wait until we hear from the royal commission. Has the Prime Minister inquired of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to see whether, at the time he was solicitor general, he was informed by anyone that electronic surveillance had been undertaken against him under the auspices of the security service of the RCMP? If he had been told that surveillance had been carried out against him and the hon. member for Nickel Belt, as stated in the allegation, what did he do about it?

I understand some information did come to the previous solicitor general, Mr. Speaker, but I am not in a position to give exact dates. I want to assure the hon. member that I regard this matter very seriously. I also await the answer to this and other questions from the present Solicitor General, who told me just before the House met that he is pursuing the inquiry.

A final supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Given the assurance that the Prime Minister is having the
Oral Questions
matter investigated, 1 would, personally, be very happy to leave it at that if he would tell me that the pending investigation by the Solicitor General and whatever checking he is doing himself would be communicated to us early next week. Will this particular aspect-namely, the involvement of the former solicitor general, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs-be reported to the House?
Mr. Speaker, I will certainly ask the present Solicitor General to take that question into very serious consideration.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, first of all 1 want to tell the honourable member that 1 appreciate very much, as I am sure do all employees of the Canadian Penitentiary Service, the motion he moved today under Standing Order 43 to show support for those public servants, and I want to thank him for that on their behalf. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to ask a supplementary question of the right hon. Prime Minister.
According to a public opinion poll made by a number of newspapers and involving 20,000 people, it would seem that 88.9 per cent of Canadians are for the reinstatement of capital punishment. This poll involved various classes of people as well as various types of crimes. 1 would like to ask the Prime Minister whether, in order to protect honest people and particularly prison guards and police forces, and to restore confidence in our judicial system, the government intends to introduce a bill during this or the next session requiring the House to vote again on the issue of capital punishment, in

February 23, 1978

response to the numerous letters we are getting from all parts of Canada?

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN GOVERNMENT SPENDING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the President of the Treasury Board. During his remarks yesterday, the President of the Treasury Board claimed that government spending had been pared to the absolute bone. However, budgetary estimates for the fiscal year 1978-79 are 13 per cent higher than budgetary estimates for fiscal 1977-78. Is the President of the Treasury Board telling the House and the country that 13 per cent is the minimum possible increase in government spending that could occur this year or could occur in the future?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (President of the Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN GOVERNMENT SPENDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my statement yesterday indicated that over-all spending for the full fiscal year 1978-79 would represent a 9.8 per cent increase at the ceiling I made public yesterday. I also indicated that the main estimates included several items which in the previous year would have been dealt with in supplementary estimates. One can think of additional funds for job creation which are in the main estimates for this year which I tabled yesterday, and which came along in supplementary form last year.
One can think of the established program finance payments to the provinces, in the order of about $550 million, which was put in the main estimates this year because we have an accurate projection on that. That is because this is the second year following the fiscal transfer arrangement. That is in the main estimates, whereas it had to be adjusted in the supplementary estimates last year. There are many items of that nature which mean that the expenditures have been moved forward to the main estimates and will not appear in the supplementary estimates. That is the simple explanation.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN GOVERNMENT SPENDING
speechtext:
The figure the President of the Treasury Board has repeated can only be arrived at through judicial assumptions as to future supplementaries and amounts that will last. It results, as well, from a $1.5 billion decrease in non-budgetary estimates, a large part of which is a result of having certain Crown corporations borrow on their own, rather than having their borrowings included in the non-budgetary estimates as has been the case in previous years.
Can the President of the Treasury Board tell us what the over-all figure would be-even using the judicial assumptions he is using-if, in fact, there had not been the structural

changes between last year and this year which, I am sure the minister will admit, distort the over-all picture and allow the production of a number like 9.8, when a considerably larger number is a more accurate description of what has happened?

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN GOVERNMENT SPENDING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would not agree with the hon. member. The structural adjustments to which I referred yesterday applied to the fiscal year 1977-78 which I clearly set before the House on February 16, 1977, when I tabled the main estimates for that year. I also said yesterday, as was pointed out by the opposition critic following my speech of February 16, 1977, that the figure for 1977-78 probably would have been about 10 per cent except for that one-time change due, again, to the fiscal transfer arrangements negotiated the previous fall. As to the other allegations of the hon. member, he is dealing very much with a hypothetical situation, and I would not attempt to play in that game.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN GOVERNMENT SPENDING
speechtext: Is the President of the Treasury Board assuring the House that exactly the same items that were included in non-budgetary estimates last fiscal year were also included in non-budgetary estimates for the coming fiscal year, and there was no change in the items that will be counted from year to year?

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN GOVERNMENT SPENDING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, one would have to follow a very detailed path through all the things dropped from one year and added to another. On balance, yes, I think they are. The hon. member for York-Simcoe pointed out, as we pointed out in the fact sheets accompanying my tabling of the main estimates yesterday, that there is borrowing by the Export Development Corporation to the extent of $365 million. We drew the attention of hon. members and the public to the fact that it is in there. We do not consider that to fall into the category the hon. member is describing, because it has a very distinct and separate purpose as to why the Export Development Corporation is going to begin to seek funds on the private market: it is related to the strategy for the Export Development Corporation.

subsubtopic: RESTRAINTS PRACTISED TO INHIBIT GROWTH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the President of the Treasury Board, seeing that we are flushing him out in terms of flim-flamming. The minister indicated that he will hold growth in the public service to six-tenths of 1 per cent, which I admit is admirable. At the same time, it has been brought to the attention of hon. members that several departments have been getting involved with temporary help and casual and term employment, which certainly has not frustrated the amount of growth in the public service: in fact, it is more.
What steps has the President of the Treasury Board taken to see that this matter has been brought to the attention of heads departments? Also, is any restraint being practised with
February 23, 1978

regard to temporary help, casual and term, or are we still going to have a lot of flim-flam in this regard?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (President of the Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: RESTRAINTS PRACTISED TO INHIBIT GROWTH
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is no flim-flam, a phrase the hon. member has fallen in love with in the last few days, obviously having picked it up from somebody else. I will be making public a complete examination of the question of temporary help, which I know has been of concern, somewhat fallaciously, to some members. I will make that release probably early next week, giving full details. I can assure the hon. member that it is under control and the representations or allegations about its misuse are, in fact, fallacious.

subsubtopic: MR. LAWRENCE-NOTICE RESPECTING QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE-ALLEGATION MINISTER MISLED HOUSE DELIBERATELY
speechtext:
I have received a notice of a question of privilege from the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence). The notice itself raises some procedural problems, some of which were raised when the hon. member rose during the question period today on a question of privilege because of a reference by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), I presume, to remarks made last night by the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham.
The notice that has been given to the Chair by the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham is as follows:
Your Honour,
Please accept this as notice that I intend to raise today at 3 p.m. a question of privilege respecting the manner in which the Minister of Finance deliberately misled the House on Monday and Tuesday of this week, as indicated in his speech to the House last evening, February 22.
Therefore, the first problem I have to deal with, which may relate to the question raised by the hon. member today in reference to the remark made by the Minister of Finance which referred back to the hon. member's speech last evening in which the same phrase "deliberately misled" was used, is

that that phrase flies directly in the face of precedents that are clearly established, that it is unparliamentary language and cannot be used by a member in this House. The reference is at page 131 of Beauchesne, citation 155(3).
In addition, I have a body of numerous references which are set out in clear and concise language by several Speakers. One I can take at random is as follows:
The hon. member for Cape Breton knows that he cannot say that another hon. member has lied to the House-that is elementary.
There are many rules which are being disregarded in the House, and just as many rules were being disregarded yesterday, but we must draw the line, and I cannot and would not want to allow an hon. member to say of another member that he has lied to the House. An hon. member cannot say of another hon. member that he has deliberately misled the House. He can say that the remarks made are perhaps incorrect, but he cannot say he has deliberately misled the House.
In light of the fact that the remarks made by the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham last night, referred to today by the Minister of Finance, and his notice today appear to fly in the face of precedents, and therefore are out of order, we have to begin by settling that procedural question first, and unless there is some argument which the hon. member can make now which would permit him to be excused from all those precedents and to use that language, when no other member has been permitted to use it in the past, I would have to find that his remarks last evening were out of order and that his notice today is out of order. Perhaps we should begin with that argument before we go on to anything else.

subsubtopic: MR. LAWRENCE-NOTICE RESPECTING QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE-ALLEGATION MINISTER MISLED HOUSE DELIBERATELY
speechtext:
I appreciate your remarks, Sir, and certainly as a member of the House I would not want to get turfed out by your edict or anyone else's. But there is a difficulty here, Sir, and it may be compounded by at least one of your own rulings. It is simply this. There are those of us on this side of the House at least, and I suspect perhaps not just confined to this side of the House, who believe that some of the things that have been said in the House about actions, activities and inactivities in respect of the dollar crisis, have not been the full truth. There may have been evasions or there may not have been evasions-we do not know-but one way of attempting to find out is to check the very obvious contradictions that have appeared in the record and to find out if some of the very obvious contradictions can be borne out one way or the other.
There can be no argument that there have been contradictions. I am fully prepared now to give at least one very obvious contradiction, and I have a motion prepared to do just that, but to be able to get to the bottom of some of those contradictions this is not the forum in which to do it. We would have to have the matter referred to a committee. In a case such as this-and I am quite open about it; this was my motive completely-the only committee I feel this matter could be referred to on a matter such as this where there are obvious contradictions by a minister of the Crown is the Standing

#

Committee on Privileges and Elections. Because of those contradictions the only way we on this side of the House would now have of raising the matter would be that hopefully a question of privilege would be raised by the other side. I think it is pertinent that that motion respecting privilege has not been made by the other side.
The reason an allegation of intent had to be made was because of a ruling from the Chair. I refer to April 19 of last year. As reported at page 4766 of Hansard, Your Honour made a ruling regarding a question of privilege. Your Honour was denying that a question of privilege had been properly raised, and in so doing this is what Your Honour said:
If it is to be pursued by way of a question of privilege, I wish to stress again that in order to qualify as a question of privilege the Chair would have to find that not only had there been actions by the minister to mislead hon. members-
That is the allegation I am making. I made it in this House during question period, and I had to repeat it again last night.
-but that those actions were calculated and deliberate by the minister for that purpose.
Sir, what sort of corner have you backed us into?

subsubtopic: MR. LAWRENCE-NOTICE RESPECTING QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE-ALLEGATION MINISTER MISLED HOUSE DELIBERATELY
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: MR. LAWRENCE-NOTICE RESPECTING QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE-ALLEGATION MINISTER MISLED HOUSE DELIBERATELY
speechtext:
The ruling of the Chair is that no one, on this type of statement which misleads members, can claim that he has a question of privilege unless he also claims that there has been a deliberate intention to mislead. On the other hand, according to the precedents-and I know them well-the Chair says that it is absolutely out of order for anyone to claim that someone has deliberately mislead the House. With respect to those two matters I believe that my privileges as a member of this House were grossly abridged because I was misled in this House by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) last Monday. The subsequent action the minister announced just 28 hours later was completely contracdictory to what he said he was going to do.
I feel that I was misled. If I was misled, my privileges and rights as a member of this House were abridged. Your Honour has said that the only way we can get that before a committee, where we could call the Governor of the Bank of Canada and where we could call members of the chartered banks of this country, is to claim that there was a deliberate intent to mislead. That is the explanation for what happened last night.
If Your Honour rules that I have to withdraw those words, I will not attempt to withdraw them in the mealy-mouthed fashion we have heard others withdraw in the last month. I will unequivocally and absolutely withdraw those words. However, I must say that by virtue of Your Honour's own ruling and under these circumstances where there is no other opportunity, in my mind, for hon. members to get to the truth of these contradictory statements by the Minister of Finance, there was no other way I know of to get the matter before that committee. Your Honour may feel that I am unfairly blaming you.

subsubtopic: MR. LAWRENCE-NOTICE RESPECTING QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE-ALLEGATION MINISTER MISLED HOUSE DELIBERATELY
speechtext:
You are.
Privilege-Mr. Lawrence

subsubtopic: MR. LAWRENCE-NOTICE RESPECTING QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE-ALLEGATION MINISTER MISLED HOUSE DELIBERATELY
speechtext:
However, I am sure Your Honour can appreciate the dilemma we are in. I have stated my motive. There is no question of what I did and how I did it, and 1 would certainly be willing to withdraw allegations of intent and deliberateness on the part of the minister if you so rule.
I still feel that no matter what type of technical language has to be used in this House, in my heart and in my mind- and I am not alone-I feel I have been misled. Knowing that, the only way we can get to the truth of the matter is to get the matter before a committee of the House.

subsubtopic: MR. LAWRENCE-NOTICE RESPECTING QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE-ALLEGATION MINISTER MISLED HOUSE DELIBERATELY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. LAWRENCE-NOTICE RESPECTING QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE-ALLEGATION MINISTER MISLED HOUSE DELIBERATELY
speechtext:
Order, please. I gave the hon. member the floor today although I could have peremptorily ruled that his remarks were unparliamentary and that they had to be withdrawn. The reason I gave him the floor on this initial problem is, as one hon. member said just a moment ago, there is a danger that it is a Catch-22 situation.
The argument put forward with all our able advisers over the last couple of hours is that it has been ruled in the past to be unparliamentary to make this kind of allegation in this language, but what happens in other situations when someone wants to bring to parliament that kind of situation in respectful terms in order to bring it to the attention of the House? If that is the case, without settling the merits I would have to hear some arguments as to whether that matter becomes procedurally barred because, if it does, it does in fact have the appearance of a Catch-22 situation. That is why I wanted to address myself primarily to the procedural problem, first of all, of whether this matter can be put forward in the terms in which the hon. member has sought to do so. I think he has given a very clear explanation of his motivation.
I may still have to come to the same decision, but I wanted to indicate that I had gone over the same argument, in my mind, as the hon. member has done, and there may be other hon. members who want to contribute to this argument now. However, it is a very serious procedural matter about which 1 would not expect to hear from hon. members unless they had had an opportunity to address themselves to the precedents with a focus on this particular aspect of the problem.
I think I should also add that I have not said from the Chair that this is the only way the matter can be approached. I said that unless this is done it certainly would not begin to qualify as a question of privilege. However, there are other procedural ways of doing the same thing, and they would have to be considered. However, I certainly would want hon. members, particularly those who have an interest in procedure, to have an opportunity to examine the precedents and to give me some assistance on whether a matter can be raised in these terms in order to have it discussed in the House, without being unparliamentary. If it cannot, we must at least know that there is some other procedure whereby matters of this kind can be brought to the floor of the House. Perhaps other hon. members wish to contribute.

February 23, 1978
Privilege-Mr. Lawrence

The words of the hon. member have to be withdrawn. The rules are clear. I do not have to go into that. The hon. member said I lied. He used words such as "deliberately", "intentionally", "overtly" and "openly". I have not lied to the House. I reported the facts as they were on Monday and on Tuesday, and I have nothing to add.
The charges of the hon. member are not true. They are not parliamentary, and I insist he withdraw them entirely.

speechtext:
I am sorry to rise again, sir, but it is on a completely separate question of privilege, the one that came up at the beginning of the question period today. I rise again more in sorrow than in anger.
I suppose at times everyone in this House under extreme pressure says things they do not really mean or do not really intend. There is a very clear imputation that, because I said what I said last night, I was not sober, i.e., I was drunk. There is a very clear imputation of that. There is no question about that at all. That was made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) in the House just a few moments ago.
Privilege-Mr. Lawrence
The reason I say I rise more in sorrow than anger is not so much for myself. I have been insulted in far better terms than that, in far better ways than that, by far better people. But when the chief financial officer of this country, under pressure, lashes out with a personal attack such as that, it does not bode good for this country or this administration. It is unparliamentary.
We have all lashed out at times. Obviously I have lashed out at times. However, I have never in my life attempted to lash out in a personal way such as that. If I have lashed out in terms uncomplimentary to anyone in public life or in private life, but especially in public life, it has been related to the public performance of the duties of that person.
I have called the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) incompetent. I have not called him drunk. I have not said to him that he has lacked sobriety in this House. I merely say to you today, Mr. Speaker, that I think that was uncalled for. I believe it to be uncomplimentary. Whether it is or is not, it does not call for a full apology. I merely say to you, sir, and through you to the Minister of Finance, that he is getting his dates and getting his parties mixed up. It is another group that was going to countenance and advocate drinking in the halls of this parliament, not this one.

speechtext: The House resumed, from Wednesday, February 22, consideration of the motion of Mr. MacEachen that Bill C-25, to establish the Northern Pipeline Agency, to facilitate the planning and construction of a pipeline for the transmission of natural gas from Alaska and northern Canada and to give effect to an agreement between Canada and the United States of America on principles applicable to such a pipeline and to amend certain Acts in relation thereto, be read the second time and referred to the special committee on a northern gas pipeline.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking on this bill this afternoon I want to outline as clearly as I possibly can the reasons why my colleagues and myself cannot accept this legislation in its present form.
The New Democratic Party has an interest in this project. We were the first political party in Canada to talk about the Alcan pipeline as being the most desirable in principle, if and when we developed the means of facilitating our American neighbours and thereby transporting American gas from Alaska to their southern markets. And, coincidentally we could provide a facility to be used in the future for transporting Canadian energy reserves from our north to the south as well.
A year ago this month the New Democratic Party said that, of all the proposals under consideration, the Alcan proposal made the most sense. The Arctic Gas proposal and the El Paso proposal had very formidable arguments to be made against them. I will not repeat those arguments now. The Alcan route, if properly implemented, had some significant advantages. It would provide for the future possibility of bringing Canadian gas to Canadian markets and thus meet Canadian needs. It was, in comparison with the other alternatives, much more desirable in terms of coping with serious issues, including native rights and environmental concerns.
This particular proposal had major benefits for the United States, and I wish to stress that. Members of my party, as with all members of the House, believe it is a normal duty for a neighbour to facilitate another neighbour whenever possible. Therefore we were entirely sympathetic toward the development of the best means, from a Canadian point of view, to aid our American neighbours in getting gas to their markets.
Before I reach the substantive benefits for Canada in this Alcan proposal I want to make it clear that this route has, as its overwhelming purpose, benefits for the United States. We should not forget that. In deciding on the Alcan route we were of course making it possible for the Americans to bring their gas from the north to the south. More particularly, in comparison to the alternatives open to the Americans, the Alcan route is some $6 billion cheaper than the El Paso route would have

been. In comparison with the Arctic gas route it is an even greater saving for the Americans. Therefore there is a major financial advantage of some $6 billion accruing to the Americans because of this proposal. By using the Alcan route the Americans will avoid a major environmental hazard of significant proportions which would have existed had they chosen the El Paso route, and which would have been inflicted upon the west coast of the United States. In choosing the Alcan route we head off that serious concern in terms of human decency and in terms of financial cost for our American neighbours.
This Alcan proposal meets with the central recommendation of the American department of defence. That department was strongly in favour of a continental route, and strongly in favour of ensuring that gas from Alaska was transported to the United States by means of a route which would have the minimum security risk in the event of a war. Obviously to send gas by tankers via the west coast, would leave their energy lines far more vulnerable to attack.
There are four important considerations to the Alcan proposal which we are debating today, and have been debating for some days, which meet American requirements. They obtain gas, it saves them $6 billion, removes an environmental risk, and it meets their military requirements; all very substantial indeed.
What are we going to get out of it as a country? About the only benefit of significance that will accrue to the people of Canada from the Alcan proposal is jobs, jobs that would accrue in the manufacturing of the pipe, in the manufacturing of steel, and jobs that would accrue on the construction site itself. In terms of these implications it is not simply Stelco, Welland, and Ipsco in Regina, it is also the other part of the steel industry in Hamilton, and in Sydney, Nova Scotia, and a component industry in Port Coquitlam in British Columbia which would benefit. In other words, if Canada received what my party believes it should receive as a minimum, that is, the guarantee of labour needed to produce the steel, the labour needed to construct the pipeline for all of the portion of the pipeline in Canada, then the benefits would have been substantial. It would also have a beneficial effect on most of the provinces right across the country, directly and indirectly.
When the Deputy Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. MacEachen) reported last September 9, after negotiations with the United States, that the Government of Canada had agreed on the Alcan route, on behalf of my colleagues I said, and said with pleasure, that I agreed to the proposal that it would produce a substantial number of jobs, as it was described by the Deputy Prime Minister. He assured us at that time, and had statistics to prove it, that the minimum Canadians would get from this project would be 100,000 man-years in jobs. Well, that is a lot of jobs, particularly at a time when a million and half in real numbers are unemployed.
Almost within days of this announcement doubts began to be raised concerning the credibility of the minister's promises. I repeat the minister did not say that we might get, we could get, or if possible we should get 100,000 man-years; he said
February 23, 1978

with great assurance and confidence on September 9 that Canadians would get 100,000 man-years in jobs.
On behalf of myself, my research staff talked with the commissioner in charge of this project in order to receive a breakdown of this estimate. The minister has refused either to deny or confirm the estimate. Perhaps sometime today the minister will let the House know about the accuracy of this contention. The commissioner in charge of the project indicated that the job estimate was based on Canada receiving 98 per cent, and not 90 per cent, of the orders for the steel necessary for the construction of the Canadian portion of the pipeline. Without that 98 per cent, we would not receive the 100,000 man-years in jobs promised by the minister. Shortly after we received that promise, we had some doubt because of the information given to us by the commissioner. We heard there would be no written guarantees in the legislation.
When the treaty came out and we saw the legislation, we realized there was no guarantee of jobs for Canadians. Actually we looked for that commitment, among other things. As other hon. members have pointed out during the course of this debate, the legislation has the treaty embodied in it. That makes sense. At least there is some logical consistency. The crucial portion of the treaty was clause 7, which is the sellout clause in terms of Canadian interest.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: Right on.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
I hear the hon. member agreeing with what I am saying. I hope he keeps that in mind when he votes later today.
Clause 7 of the treaty should have provided Canadians with an exclusive right to the production of steel and the construction of the pipeline, but there is no such provision. In fact that clause is almost exactly the opposite. The provision in clause 7 indicates that if Canadians are fortunate enough, in terms of meeting international competition, they will have the legal right to compete in order to get jobs on the Canadian portion of the pipeline.
Because of the pipeline, the Americans will save $6 billion, lessen environmental risk to their west coast, and will have their defence needs met. The minister negotiated for Canadians to have the right to do work on the pipeline after world competition. I consider that clause to be a sellout clause. It was produced by a minister who sold out the interests of Canadian workers, when the treaty was negotiated. All negotiations involve a little give and take. Throughout our history, whenever Liberals do negotiating on behalf of Canadians, Canadians do the giving and Americans do the taking. This legislation is a beautiful example of that.
I am somewhat concerned about what has been indicated by the official opposition. The hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) can argue with brilliant legalistic persuasion on both sides of any cause. He outdid himself in this debate. He devoted half of his time to attacking the New Democratic Party, which I found curious. My party was the first party
Northern Pipeline
which advocated this pipeline route. We have remained consistent by indicating that Canadians should receive the jobs to which they are entitled. Instead of zeroing in on the government, he spent the first half of his speech attacking my party. Having done that, then he proceeded to point out the faults in the bill. That is a perfect example of bad conscience. I will not bore the House or the hon. member by quoting his words. Hearing them once was bad enough. He went on at great length to indicate what a deplorable piece of legislation this was. He concluded his speech by saying that of course the Conservative party would vote for it.

speechtext: After it is amended.

speechtext:
Yes, that was the position. I do not want to quote just the hon. member for the Yukon. I give credit to the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) who comes from a steel community. He was in on the issue early. He indicated what was involved as a possible benefit for Canada in terms of jobs. Like hon. members of the New Democratic Party, he stressed the positive possibilities. I wish he would take a consistent position, as hon. members of my party do. Then when the hon. member for Hamilton West saw the bill, he was horrified and had some rather uncomplimentary things to say about the government. He indicated that what was involved was "a sellout to the American consumer at the expense of Canadian steelworkers and jobs for Canadians."
Also he indicated that there should be guarantees in order to protect the interests of our steel industry and those who provide goods and services, which play a major part in this pipeline. He went on to say that there had to be such guarantees before this piece of legislation would be worthy of support. I am not frequently persuaded by the arguments of the hon. member for Hamilton West. We differ quite often, but in this instance I found his logic rather cogent and his argument sound. This legislation, without guarantees, is certainly unworthy of support.
I want to say to the hon. member for Hamilton West, the hon. member for the Yukon, and the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), as well as to all other Conservative members who have opposed this bill, that their arguments are sound. I hope when my party votes against this bill that those hon. members will join with us in voting against a piece of legislation which is a sellout of Canadian interests.
I have some fresh details which I should like to add to the debate. The government has made the argument that the Canadian steel industry is efficient, modern, and competent. Indeed it is. In fact it is one of the few sectors in the manufacturing end of things which is of world quality. The Canadian steel industry deserves a lot of credit for having entrepreneurial initiative, and for knowing when to renew its capital equipment. That industry is a credit to the country. It shows us the modern industrial base that can be created in Canada.
However, the conclusion drawn from this by the government, simply because they are competitive and efficient, is that we should blindly assume that that industry will receive the
3206

February 23, 1978
Northern Pipeline
orders. We should assume that it will follow, as night follows day, that jobs will inevitably occur in the communities I referred to earlier in my speech. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that that does not necessarily follow at all, and I will give six interconnected reasons for Canadians right now being skeptical about the possibility of getting anywhere near the number of jobs the Deputy Prime Minister has said we will get.
First, I refer the Deputy Prime Minister to a study that was done by an interdepartmental committee in the United States, a study which the minister said the other day he had not read, when I mentioned it out in the question period. In that study the U.S. authorities claim that, in their view at least, 30 per cent of the business for the Canadian portion of the pipeline will go to the United States. That is considerably more than the minister has contended. That is not a study produced by the NDP or by some fly-by-night organization, but one produced by an interdepartmental committee of the United States.
Second-and I mentioned this to the minister a long time ago-the Bank of America in the United States has been running adds, not simply in the Wall Street Journal, which I know the minister reads with interest, but in many cases right across the United States. The assumption of the Bank of America is exactly the same as that of the interdepartmental committee, that they anticipate that at least 30 per cent of the business for the Canadian portion of the pipeline will go to the United States.
Third, if the minister is not persuaded by the Americans, as he usually is-they usually do an effective job on him and then they tell him what a tough negotiator he is, and when the Americans tell him what a good job he has done, then we can be sure we have lost completely-then I refer him to one of his own department's studies. DREE did a study for the government on this pipeline in which they said that unless there were assurances about jobs we would get nowhere near the number of jobs the minister has been promising. In fact the part of the estimates on which the minister has been relying for his job prognostications is what DREE called "the wish book", which the Deputy Prime Minister has inflicted upon Canada as being a guarantee for Canadian jobs.
This is what the study said:
Unless there are effective controls ensuring Canadian content, 67 per cent may be a more realistic projection.
That is 67 per cent only of the jobs, not anywhere near the 90 per cent to 98 per cent, depending on which figure the minister deems to be appropriate at the time, which he has been promising the people of Canada.
Some people might ask what is the difference between 67 per cent and what the minister has promised. It involves about $600 million worth of business less than the minister has been telling Canadians we will get. If you translate the $600 million into jobs, it could mean we will get thousands fewer jobs, according to the DREE study, than the minister has said we will get. So we are not talking about a handful of dollars or a

mere scattering of jobs; we are talking about thousands of jobs and hundreds of millions of dollars about which the minister had been warned by a department of which he should know something.
Fourth, when we are talking about the competitive situation and how likely we are to get these jobs in Canada, we have to consider the state of the world's steel industry, the very people with whom we will be competing. As even the minister should probably know by now, demand has fallen off very considerably throughout the world in terms of steel, but simultaneously capacity in the steel producing countries has grown considerably.
Excess steel supplies have caused world prices to tumble all over, driving many producers into the red. For example, the five largest Japanese steel companies reported combined losses of over $300 million in the first six months of the fiscal year ending in September of last year. A similar situation exists with the British steel industry. The reality is that the steel industry in Japan, in Britain, in the United States, and in Italy, is in a state of slump. It is looking for new markets and it will be concentrating on the Alcan project as a major instrument of bailing itself out.
I should like to quote two of the principals involved in this whole issue, the heads of companies in Canada. The minister is fond of saying the steel industry is confident so why is the NDP not confident? I repeat that we are confident about the steel industry in Canada; we just have no confidence in the government.
Mr. John Allen, president of Stelco, said recently:
The realities of the current world steel environment are such that Canadian producers will have to fight as never before for future orders and overcome fierce competition from overseas manufacturers, most of whom operate in countries whose governments use their industrial infrastructures as an employment-providing or foreign-exchange-generating mechanism.
Not long ago I met Mr. Jim MacLennan, president of Ipsco, and discussed the situation with him. He made essentially the same point, and in fact went on the record on the night that the National Energy Board made its ruling on the size of the pipe. I heard him on the radio, and I am sure he was on television the same night, saying he has a great deal of concern about the Japanese, the Italians and other steel makers in the world, getting contracts. He spoke with confidence, as he should have, about his own company, because it has done a damn good job, just as Mr. John Allen, head of Stelco, spoke with confidence about his own company. But neither of these individuals underestimate the problems that will occur for Canada in getting those contracts, in a world community in which the steel industry is now operating way under capacity and is looking for new orders.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) dealt most specifically with the problem of competition. He dealt most specifically with the variety of means open to other companies in other countries to undercut the Canadian suppliers. A whole variety of methods can be used to undercut the competitive regulation which is supposed to be in
February 23, 1978

the legislation. I appeal to the Deputy Prime Minister to consider this argument when he winds up the debate.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner), speaking in the debate on Monday, February 20, replied to the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands. I was astounded to read his speech and I am totally convinced the minister made a mistake when he read the notes that were prepared for him by his department, because in one paragraph he put forward an argument which he withdrew completely in the next. I refer the Deputy Prime Minister to page 3035 in Hansard. It is at this point that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce is trying to deal with the fundamental argument which is now of concern to the leaders of the steel industry in Canada and to members of the NDP, that is, the problem of assessing what fair competition is in reaching a decision about which companies in which parts of the world are going to get contracts. This is what he said in terms of dealing with state subsidies, special tax concessions of the kind, for example, that DISC provides in the United States:
Action under the Anti-dumping Act could be taken in cases where exports into Canada are financed under more favourable terms than are available to the foreign manufacturer for its domestic sales. Under regulation (11 A) of the anti-dumping regulations, credit and other financing terms can be taken into account in determining the normal value, export price, and, hence, the margins of dumping under the meaning of the act.
That quote, if left alone, might persuade a number of people in this House. People might say that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce has shown that we have regulations which will really protect the Canadian steel industry from unfair competition. However, the minister went on, and as sure as I stand here I am totally convinced the minister made a mistake. I think he was reading a note from one of his officials about the problem associated with this, because this is how the minister continued:
It should be noted that neither (11 A) of the anti-dumping regulations nor the imposition of countervailing duties for reasons of export financing subsidies, appear to have been tested as yet. Moreover, the anti-dumping option would really only come into play after the fact, which renders its use, other than as a threat mechanism, somewhat ineffective.
The Deputy Prime Minister looked concerned when I read that to him, and well he should, because in the words of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce there is a complete undermining of the government's argument that we are going to be protected. What the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce said is that the very provisions of the Anti-dumping Act in section (11A) are going to be ineffective. He was saying that they have not as yet been tested and that with regard to the Alcan pipeline they would become operative only after the fact. Does this mean that after we buy the pipe and lay it- whether we buy it from Italy, Japan or some other country which might win in the bidding-only then can the government go back and say, "Too bad, fellows, you violated our anti-dumping legislation"?
I repeat what the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce said:
Northern Pipeline
Moreover, the anti-dumping option would really only come into play after the fact, which renders its use, other than as a threat mechanism, somewhat ineffective.
That was not said by a member of the opposition, it was said by a minister of the Crown, and to me it is the most damning argument which has been presented on the matter of competitiveness. I hope the Deputy Prime Minister will deal with that issue when he speaks.
With regard to being optimistic that Canadians will get the jobs in a competitive situation, the minister said that the Canadian steel industry is competitive. We think it is competitive, but who got the contracts for building the American pipeline in Alaska? Was it the Canadian steel industry or the American steel industry? Not at all. It was the Japanese steel industry. I do not know why the minister is so convinced that we will automatically get the contracts to produce the pipe when, for a similar project in Alaska, the Japanese, not the Canadians or the Americans, got the contracts. Surely that should give even the minister reason to pause and not be so acquiescent and optimistic about jobs.
Financial experts are now saying that Foothills will find it easier and cheaper to finance the project if more pipe, equipment and services are purchased offshore than originally planned. Lacking government financial backstopping which would have increased security and lowered debt costs, the consortium may be forced to minimize debt costs as much as possible to ensure debt and equity financing. One obvious way of achieving this would be to take advantage of less expensive foreign export financing which often accompanies foreign purchases.
If the consortium attempts to raise funds abroad, perhaps either in Japan or Europe, in the face of financing difficulties here in North America, it could well expect demands by foreign bankers and other foreign investors that the project use foreign funds to purchase foreign goods and services. In other words, if Foothills is going to get assistance in financing this massive project, which will cost anywhere from $10 billion to $14 billion, the source of those funds, whether continental Europe or Japan, could well insist that a good part of that money be used to purchase equipment in those countries. This is not a concern expressed only by the New Democratic Party.
I want to read to the minister from a confidential report prepared by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. With direct reference to this problem of financing abroad, and therefore buying steel abroad, the report says the following:
The Canadian content actually achieved could vary substantially from estimates because of competitive pricing conditions, tied and concessional Financing, government monitoring, corporate attitudes, and other factors.
The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce seems quite concerned about tied and concessional financing arrangements which could be made by Foothills in and with other countries.

When he has the opportunity to stand up and be counted, he does what he often does-turns the other cheek.
I believe this is an excellent amendment. If parliament rules that all the employment for manufacture of the pipe, the valves, digging the holes, laying the pipe, constructing the pumping stations and other facilities, should be Canadian, the only people in trouble will be those who sign the treaty and the amendments that will be made to it.

A lot of things have not been said. I would be surprised if a great deal of money is not tied up in the development of the pipeline which may not be built for many years, or even not at all. The hon. member for the Yukon is aware of what is happening to the gas coming from Alaska today. He knows that much of it is being shipped to Japan. He knows that if we allow gas to be shipped to Japan by the United States, the consequences to our competitive position will be great. Japan will get cheap gas because it is not very far from Alaska and will not cost much to transport. The gas will then be used for the manufacture of steel. We are in the unhappy position of having to haul coal from Hamilton or other places, and so would not be competitive.
The hon. member is well aware that more gas is being developed in western Canada than we need today. There are applications galore before the National Energy Board to sell more gas. We are not concerned with a pipeline that is needed in a great rush. We will be able to demand time to develop the pipe, the valves, the pumping stations and all the necessary infrastructure if we make these things a condition of allowing the United States to transport fuel across our nation.

The hon. member for the Yukon knows that there was no opportunity in Alaska for training local people and that most of the labour was imported. He knows that other American states were not allowed to bid on the pipe. The pipe came from Japan. In fact it was manufactured years before the decision was made with regard to the pipeline. It sat there rusting. He knows that.
The hon. member cannot have it both ways. If he believes the Liberal party is the big business party, he should join them. However, he will find that both those parties are losing a lot of friends. When my leader gets so close enough to and knowledgeable about the corporations that the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) begins calling them our "corporate chums," he may be closer than he thinks. We are talking about steel plants in Canada, workers who will work on the pipeline, and those who have not yet been trained to work on the pipeline. The hon. member knows that the facilities are not yet built. We have the capability and the know-how. All we need is time to develop the design and we will build the valves for the 56-inch pipeline. These valves are not available anywhere in the world. Given the opportunity, we can build them as good as or better than any country.
I may agree to a road being built across my farm and what the terms of the lease and so on will be. Obviously I will request that I not only have the right to use that road, but to be employed to maintain it and snowplough it. I will either demand that I provide that kind of labour, or get a tax reduction. That would be anticipated. With regard to the pipeline, the Americans can expect no less from us.

Because we are good neighbours we are making certain concessions. In return, we will ask for concessions.

He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill has been in the works for almost two years. It was dealt with in the other place, received third reading, and as a result has come to this place. that Bill S-6, to provide an exception from the public general law relating to marriage in the case of Fran$ois Eugene Arthur Waddell and Marie Anne Marguerite Benoit, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills and Standing Orders.
Marriage Law Exceptions
He said: Mr. Speaker, the bill seeks an exception from the general law regarding the degrees of affinity within which two people may marry. The petitioner, Eugene Waddell, wishes to marry his niece, Marguerite Benoit.
The preamble to the bill, which will be proven in committee, sets out the pertinent facts showing the necessity for bringing the bill before parliament.
Prior to the framing of the British North America Act in 1967, the civil code of the province of Quebec of 1866 was in effect, and it contains the provisions saying that a man may not marry his niece. The next year the British North America Act gave legislative jurisdiction to the Parliament of Canada in the Field of marriage and, to the provinces, legislative jurisdiction in the field of solemnization of marriage. However, the degrees of consanguinity are part of the law of marriage rather than part of the law of solemnization of marriage, and therefore only the Parliament of Canada may properly legislate in this regard. The prohibition against marriage between uncle and niece contained in the code is therefore a matter of federal legislative jurisdiction. Because that prohibition was in the civil code of 1866, Section 129 of the British North America Act keeps it in force until it is "repealed, abolished or altered" by the Parliament of Canada.
Since the Parliament of Canada has exclusive jurisdiction in respect of marriage and since, under Section 129 of the BNA Act, it has the power to "repeal or amend" the law that was in force in Quebec at the time of Confederation, I submit that it has the power to pass a private bill permitting the petitioners to marry each other, notwithstanding the prohibition that would otherwise make it impossible for them to marry.
I do not propose to go into any detail save to note that the petitioner, Eugene Waddell, is 84 years of age, and Miss Benoit is 66.
At this time I would like to express my appreciation on their behalf of the co-operation of the House leaders. I am sure all members would like to wish them much love and happiness in the years ahead.

Mr. Speaker, in that connection I should like to point out that this amendment does not send the bill to the committee but, rather, sends its subject matter. Therefore the limitations that apply to amending a bill at second reading in my view do not apply. If on second reading we were trying to amend clauses of the bill, I know it could be argued from the authorities that the thing to do for that is to wait until we get the bill into committee. However, in this case we are sending the subject matter rather than the bill itself.
There is a rather long paragraph on page 185 of Beau-chesne's Fourth Edition which is part of citation 226(2). The opening lines talk about the subject matter of a bill and so on, and then we get down to the last dozen lines:
Northern Pipeline
Accordingly, an instruction can be moved that authorizes the introduction of amendments into a Bill which extend its provisions to objects not contained therein, if those objects are relevant to the subject-matter thereof, or which would augment the legislative machinery whereby the Bill is to be put into force; whilst, on the other hand, no instruction is permissible which is irrelevant, foreign, or contradictory to the contents of the Bill, or that seeks the subversion thereof, by substituting another scheme for the mode of operation therein prescribed.
According to Dr. Beauchesne, that was taken from some edition of May at pages 398 and 399. There are other citations on other pages. I go back to page 183, citation 221(1).
The object of a permissive instruction-
That is what this is, sir, not a mandatory instruction. It is a permissive instruction that the committee has power to consider such and such. Surely the power to consider such and such is not a mandatory instruction.
The objective of a permissive instruction, which is the more ordinary form, is to confer on the Committee authority to do something which, without the ins'.ruction, they would have no power to do, for example, to divide a bill into two bills, to consolidate two bills into one, or to extend the scope of a bill. Instructions of this kind merely empower the Committee to take the course of action specified, leaving it to the discretion of the Committee whether or not they exercise the power.
What is proposed in the amendment is not that the bill be divided or anything like that, but that its scope be extended, and I have in mind the limitation that was in the citation I read earlier, that that extension cannot go beyond the objectives of the bill. I suggest that the whole question of this bill providing jobs for Canadians and providing for the production of pipe in Canada is not foreign to-it is part of-the bill. It is part of what was talked about in the treaty and so forth, so we are simply extending the provisions of the bill to provide that with respect to these matters, the making of the pipe and the providing of jobs, there shall be certain guarantees.
As I say, the requirement that we cannot be foreign to the bill, it seems to me, is met in this amendment. It deals with writing into the bill guarantees about things that are already implicit in it. And as for the suggestion that the instruction is mandatory, I do not see how that can be taken seriously at all because it is an instruction of a permissive nature, giving the committee the right to make recommendations for the inclusion in the said bill of certain guarantees. Surely that is leaving it to the committee, in the terms of citation 221, whether or not they exercise that power.
While it is a bit unusual as an amendment and perhaps a bit innovative in that we are sending the subject matter rather than the bill-and we frequently have had amendments sending subject matter-it seems to me to be in line with the other citations, namely, the right to ask the committee to consider recommending that certain clauses be put into the bill in the nature of guarantees.

There are several other precedents that indicate an instruction is out of order if it attempts to introduce into a bill a subject which should properly form the substance of a distinct measure.
Page 513 of Erskine May's nineteenth edition covers the points raised by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen), that is to say, that since the clauses of a bill can be amended to accomplish what it is endeavoured to accomplish by the general amendment, that the amendment goes beyond the scope of a proper amendment at second reading stage and gets into amendments that can and properly should be secured by specific clause by clause amendments when the bill is in committee.

1 wish to refer to a statement made today in the debate and earlier by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) to the effect that the only significiant benefit to Canada in the Alcan pipeline project is jobs that may occur in the country. Of course, there is a benefit to Canada from jobs that we expect to be created. However, there are other benefits. It would be a great mistake for anyone, especially for anyone in the House of Commons, to believe that the only significiant benefit to Canada from this international enterprise is the creation of jobs, admitting the vital importance of that result.
I should begin by saying that this is an international project. It will be the result of an agreement that was negotiated between Canada and the United States. It was understood from the beginning that neither country could enter into the

February 23, 1978
Northern Pipeline
agreement unless it could register definite benefits for itself from the agreement.
In the negotiations we were seeking mutual benefits, benefits for the United States and benefits for Canada. I am not put off or disturbed in any way if members, especially those in the New Democratic Party, say in comparison that the El Paso route of Mr. Schlesinger was able to give a benefit of $8 billion to the United States as opposed to the Alcan route. Obviously there were strong pressures in the United States for that domestic route and not an international route. It had to be defended in the United States because that choice yielded benefits to the United States. Therefore, I do not regard that as a convincing argument against entering into this agreement. I refer to the argument that the United States gained benefits.
This agreement has provided benefits for the United States and is providing benefits for Canada. It is a plus for both Canada and the United States. I want to list as briefly as possible the main benefits that are accruing to Canada as a result of this agreement.
First, the agreement provides access to western Arctic supplies of gas on the only economic basis currently available to meet growing needs in this country. The capacity for the transmission of Canadian gas would be 1.2 billion cubic feet per day and even a flow of as little as 800 million cubic feet daily would be sufficient to supply up to 10 per cent of the forecast demand for several years. In contrast, the larger supplies in Alaska would only supply 5 per cent of United States needs.
Second, as a result of the cost-sharing formula with the United States with regard to the Dempster lateral, as provided for in the agreement, the cost of transporting Canadian gas could be up to 20 cents per mcf less than under the original National Energy Board proposal for a diversion of the main line in the Yukon to Dawson. That could represent a saving for the transport of existing Canadian reserves of $1 billion.
Third, it is estimated that between $4 billion and $5 billion will be spent in Canada in current dollar terms for the purchase of goods and services required for the construction of the 2,765 mile pipeline system from the Yukon to the southern U.S. border. These estimates do not include the lateral. This includes everything from design, engineering, projection supervision and transportation of supplies and equipment to pipes, valves, compressors, flanges and construction machinery. These outlays will provide a substantial boost to output and employment in this country, not only as a result of direct spending on the pipeline itself and all the machinery and equipment required to build and operate it, but also because of indirect demand for other goods and services that will be generated by pipeline spending.
Fourth, as stated previously on many occasions, nearly
100,000	man-years of employment would be created by the total project including the Delta lateral. Some 69,000 man-years would be generated directly by construction activities and 31,000 man-years indirectly as a result of expenditures of pipeline income. That was the estimate that was given when the agreement was announced. It was the estimate that we

have been working on. Later I will deal with some of the interconnected reasons that the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby put before the House.
Fifth, the construction of the pipeline system and the guaranteed access it assures to the Mackenzie Delta as a result of the Foothills commitment to provide a connecting lateral will provide substantial stimulus to continued exploration for new petroleum reserves in the western Arctic.
Sixth, the northern pipeline project will have a strongly positive impact on Canada's international balance of payments. That has hardly been mentioned in the debate. The first boost will come from the expected heavy inflow of capital to help finance construction in Canada, and once the gas begins to flow through the line to the south, Canada will be in receipt of substantial payments from the U.S. to cover transmission charges.
It is interesting that this particular aspect of the pipeline agreement was mentioned specifically at the federal-provincial conference of first ministers by Premier Allan Blakeney, whom the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby recommended to us as the only man at the first ministers' conference who could assist the current economic situation in Canada. He ruled out the provinces of Ontario, British Columbia and Manitoba but he selected the premier of Saskatchewan as the paragon of economic analysis. Obviously what he said would be acceptable to the hon. member. At pages 13 and 14 of his address concerning the Alcan project, he was talking about energy projects in general and I quote the premier:
While it's not an energy project for Saskatchewan, the Alcan pipeline project is key. That project awaits a number of very important decisions.
The pipeline could mean 18,000 man-years of construction work and 1,000 permanent jobs.
The premier of Saskatchewan is obviously referring to his province. Then he goes on to say that fees for Alaska gas flowing to the United States through the pipeline could earn Canada as much as $800 million a year by 1983. That is a very substantial benefit. Every year by 1983 American shippers or purchasers will pay Canada $800 million. Then he goes on to say:
If the federal government makes sure that the pipe can be made in Canada, the steel plant in Regina could expand its capacity creating both construction work and nearly 500 permanent jobs.
You will notice that the premier of Saskatchewan said "if the federal government makes sure that the pipe can be made in Canada". We have assured that. The National Energy Board through its recommendation has assured the premier of Saskatchewan that the pipe can be made in Canada. I am sure that the premier of Saskatchewan, even though he is not a graduate of the London School of Economics, knows the difference between the words "can" and "will". He is a graduate of Dalhousie University. That is why I put high value on his selection of words. I will return to the premier of Saskatchewan's remarks later on because I find his speech rich in analysis which will, of course, be immediately accepted by

the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby who extolled his qualities yesterday in the debate.
I mentioned the support on the point of the balance of payments. The premier said that fees for Alaska gas flowing to the United States through the pipeline could earn Canada as much as $800 million a year by 1983. By the way, that figure is substantiated by the National Energy Board, and that is a powerful assistance to Canada.
Here I address myself to the hon. member for Yukon on the question of Yukon employment. Foothills have indicated that preference will be given to Yukon residents in hiring for construction of the line. It is estimated that some 200 permanent jobs will be opened up to residents of the Yukon to oversee operation of the pipeline in the territory and that many hundreds more will be created indirectly in the north as a result of the catalytic effect of the project in stimulating continued petroleum exploration and in helping to foster other industrial development.
I am disappointed that the chief spokesman for the New Democratic Party, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) and the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby, have confined their interest in the pipeline basically to that part of Ontario which is so interesting to the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby. Not a word about the industrial possibilities and employment opportunities that will come in the Yukon as a result of the catalytic effect of the project.

go around saying the only significant benefit to Canada is from jobs we have not guaranteed.
Here is a very significant benefit to the Yukon under the agreement with the United States. The company will be required to pay property taxes of $35 million prior to completion of the line and $30 million annually thereafter, an amount which increases each year in line with the gross national product price deflator. Assuming 5 per cent inflation, net property tax payments of the company in the Yukon over the 25 year period will be more than $1 billion.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands said we threw away a $200 million compensation fund. He said our chief negotiator threw away a $200 million card that he did not have to throw away. I admit I threw away that $200 million card, but I played a more than $1 billion card for the Yukon. This reminds me of what Mr. Lysyk and the National Energy Board recommended. What has been negotiated has yielded the Yukon more than three times the amount that would have been yielded to the Yukon under the National Energy Board proposal, three times more than what was suggested and recommended by the National Energy Board, and twice as much as was recommended by Dean Lysyk.
By this negotiation the property taxes we have achieved for the Yukon over the lifetime of the pipeline will amount to net tax revenues of more than $1 billion, which are much greater than any recommendation given to us by the National Energy Board and by Dean Lysyk.
In addition to the property taxes which will be paid to the Yukon, there is the very substantial revenue which will flow into the treasuries of the three western provinces as a result of the pipeline from such levies as property taxes and personal and corporate income taxes. Also the federal government will reap significant revenue from all these sources, other than property taxes.
If one compiles the benefits Canada will receive as a result of this agreement, one will see that the question of jobs is an important part but not the only part of the total benefits accruing to Canada.
I thank the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) for the general support his party has given to this bill. I should like to answer a number of his criticisms. He indicated that the government has delayed the bringing in of this legislation. We brought the legislation in after having put the complex elements together. It was necessary to decide that before bringing in the legislation. It is true the United States Congress dealt quickly with the decision of the President. That was so because of pre-legislation which had been passed earlier under the Alaska natural gas transportation act. The United States Congress still has to deal with the President's energy package before gas contracts can be finalized. I am told these contracts are vital to the financing of the project.
The question of the price of gas in the United States has to be resolved. As yet the United States has not set up any administrative mechanism, nor any regulatory authority to
