deal with the pipeline. All of these things must be done. There is no basis for the complaint by the hon. member that the government is delaying the commencement of this project. The passage of this legislation is timely. If it can be dealt with in committee, then we will be in phase with the requirements as they have developed.
Also the hon. member for the Yukon dealt with the wide powers which were being given to the pipeline agency. These powers would be given directly and indirectly through the authority of the governor in council to amend regulations under other acts relating to the pipeline, or to transfer powers under legislation which bear on the project. I had that very much in mind when I was building the legislative framework.
During the debate which occurred last August, the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) indicated that as a final condition for approval of the Foothills project his party insisted upon the creation of a single authority or independent regulatory agency. Also he indicated that the agency should be new and only last for the life of the project. That is what we are providing for. He continued by saying that the agency should have clear authority over all agencies and departments whose conflicts now complicate life in the north. He suggested that this agency must have a mandate to oversee and regulate technical and social problems connected with the pipeline. That is exactly what the government has attempted to do. We wanted to create a single authority which would be capable of overseeing and regulating the technical and social problems connected with the pipeline.

I will say that the hon. member for Yukon seemed to be somewhat ambivalent about his position on the provisions of the bill with respect to judicial reports. On the one hand he expressed concern that Indian groups may make every effort to prevent the project from proceeding, and he said he does not agree with that. On the other hand, he is concerned also about the denial of the fundamental right in British justice of guaranteeing a citizen free access to the courts.
In the course of his remarks the hon. member suggested that I had unintentionally misled the House in asserting that the restrictions on the judicial process proposed in the bill were

similar to those provided by the United States with respect to the pipeline project. I believe that many of the restrictions are similar, but I did not mean, and I do not mean now, to suggest that they were identical. As the hon. member said, the court of appeal in the district of Columbia may quash, alter or confirm an order of the regulatory authority. He suggested that the courts in Canada had the power to confirm, quash, alter or refer back the decision of the semi-judicial tribunal.
He went on to contend, as I understood him, that clause 23 would be more acceptable if the appellate tribunal were empowered not only to confirm or refer back an order of the National Energy Board or the designated officer in the agency but also to alter it. I am informed by others more learned in the law than 1 that in fact it is not customary in Canadian practice to authorize the courts to vary the decision of an administrative agency of this nature. I suggest, therefore, that this is a matter which must be weighed more carefully in considering where to strike a balance which ensures the preservation of justice and equity for the individual without unnecessarily or unreasonably obstructing the progress of a project which promises so much benefit for the vast majority of the Canadian people.
Now I would like, if I may, Mr. Speaker, to turn to a number of questions involving the pipeline project as it affects the Yukon territory. It has been suggested that I made somewhat wild statements regarding preference for Yukon labour and procurement. The legislation requires the company to comply with undertakings it made before the National Energy Board which include a clear commitment to give preference to Yukon residents in hiring and procurement. Northern Pipeline
There were a number of references made throughout the debate to various proposals that were put forward earlier with regard to providing additional funding for the benefit of the Yukon. This question was thoroughly covered by my colleague, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Faulkner). 1 think it might be worth reiterating the $200 million heritage fund recommended by the Lysyk inquiry, which the hon. member for Yukon described as up front money to meet the additional costs that the territory would face as a result of the project of providing additional services and facilities. The hon. member for Yukon argued that the provision we have made for the Yukon to borrow up to $200 million between 1978 and 1982 was back-end money.
I think it ought to be made clear that the heritage fund proposed by the Lysyk inquiry was not intended to provide up-front money to meet additional costs of services and facilities required by the pipeline but was for quite unrelated purposes. The provision permitting the Yukon to borrow up to $200 million would make funds available for this very purpose.
I dealt earlier with the suggestion made by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands that when we agreed in the negotiations to forego the idea of a $200 million fund we threw away a valuable card. I have already indicated that that is nonsense.
Instead of gaining the $200 million so-called compensation fund for the Yukon we suggested in the negotiations the payment of a property tax to accrue to the treasury of the Yukon more than $1 billion over the lifetime of the pipeline. So I do not feel there is a need for going into that question more thoroughly.
I am satisfied that anyone who looks at the report of Lysyk and the funding recommendations of the National Energy Board for the Yukon, including the heritage fund, and at what has been negotiated, would agree that we have in all cases enriched the situation for the Yukon considerably above any proposals that were made by these inquiries.
The question of a further examination of the socio-economic impact of the project on the Yukon was dealt with in considerable detail by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. As he made clear in response to unwarranted allegations of a number of members of the opposition, this second stage examination of the issues involved will provide a full opportunity for public consideration and discussion.
The second stage examination will be undertaken by the northern pipeline agency, and it will focus on the detailed terms and conditions which will be imposed on the company to maximize the benefits and minimize the adverse effects of the pipeline, which the Lysyk inquiry emphasized should be the principal objective of the exercise.
A number of speakers, notably the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) and the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes), raised the question of socio-economic considerations as they apply to northeastern British Columbia. I appreciate the concerns which hon. members have

That refrain has been echoed mainly by members of the New Democratic Party who exhibit an innate sense of inferiority which they feel as a result of the long period spent in their particular part of the House of Commons. I feel no such sense of inferiority even though, as the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) suggested this afternoon, I ought to feel it because 1 come from a "backward part" of Canada.
In this debate I have been waiting to find out where we have been outslickered. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands made some comments that I will deal with in a moment. I doubt there has ever been a negotiation undertaken with the United States or any other country that has not prompted some Canadians to proclaim that Canada got the worst of the bargain.
The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) had an unhappy complaint about all the instances in history when poor Canada had been outslickered by the United States. I find it rather interesting that some in the United States Congress seem to believe the same thing-but in the opposite way. They have been complaining that their negotiators ought to go back to Canada and improve the result obtained on the question of content, because it was obvious they had been outslickered by those shrewd Canadian negotiators.
I want to spend a moment or two with the arguments advanced by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands in support of his allegation that we had been outslickered by those shrewd Yankee negotiators. His speech wavered between an expression of fear of the United States and an expression of disdain for the United States. He was not sure on which side he came down. As I understood his case, it rested on the contention that the United States desperately need the pipeline while Canada would not require gas from the Mackenzie Delta much before the mid-1990s, and might not need it
Northern Pipeline
at all until early next century. His analysis is now supported by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby. I do not know what he will say when I point out later that the paragon of economic analysis, the premier of Saskatchewan, disagreed with that view quite openly at the federal-provincial conference.
The hon. member said that Canada was put on the defensive by stressing the need to gain access to our Delta reserves, to which he would have attached a low priority. He would have attached a low priority to Canada's gaining access to our Delta reserves-I think that is important-and if not a low priority, no priority at all.
He went on to say that the Canadian bargaining position was strengthened because the United States desperately needed the gas and we do not. We had a further bargaining point because the United States would save $6 billion by transporting existing reserves by the overland route as opposed to the United States alternative, which apparently horrified their military authorities for security reasons.
Out of this fabricated "made in Canada" content policy the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands tried to build his argument. While he now tells us that the United States desperately needs access to Alaskan gas, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby told us on August 4 that there were reports put before President Carter which showed that the United States did not need the gas until the late 1980s. That is the argument he made in support of delaying the project. Now the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands says they desperately need the gas but that their military authorities were horrified at the prospect of an allAmerican route.
The hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby repeated that unfounded allegation this afternoon. We know that the President of the United States received a report from his Department of Defence. The conclusion was that of the three transportation systems there was no overriding preference for one route over another when the analysis was based on military factors alone.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands referred to the saving of $6 billion to the United States by transporting this 22 trillion cubic feet of established Alaskan reserves via the overland route. I should inform him that the saving to Canada of transporting delta reserves of some five billion cubic feet through the joint system, as opposed to the all-Canadian alternative along the Mackenzie Valley, is estimated to be in the order of $2.5 billion. In relation to the size of our reserves there, the savings to Canada on this joint project are 60 per cent greater than is the case for the United States.
When you follow the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands down the dark alleys of his arguments you find that his arguments really fall apart. Of course, we on this side of the House differ fundamentally with the New Democratic Party on the question of the critical importance to Canada of gaining access on an economic basis to our reserves in the

February 23, 1978
Northern Pipeline
western Arctic. In this we share completely the view of the Conservative party as expressed by its leader in the debate last August, when he said that the primary goal is to deliver Canadian resources to Canadian markets.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext:
My colleague the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) very carefully explained why we consider it so vital to ensure access to our reserves in the Mackenzie Delta.
During the debate last August, the leader of the New Democratic Party was so concerned about the availability of gas reserves in Canada to meet future needs that he proposed, in effect, that we take the drastic step of abrogating our contracts to supply the United States after 1985 with any exports thereafter on a swap basis only. That was the course of action recommended by the leader of that party last August. This past week their chief spokesman said that we really do not need that gas.
I believe the New Democratic Party is prepared to put the future well-being of Canadians at stake in a numbers game based on widely varying estimates from private sources. We are not prepared to join the New Democratic Party in that particular gamble.
I wish to refer to the speech made by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources in which he underlined the importance to Canada of gaining access to Canadian gas in order to reduce our dependence on imported oil. In that connection, I wish to refer to what the premier of Saskatchewan said at the federal-provincial conference. I quote:
-I can't think of a better place for governments to start investing in our future than in energy. Jobs today-energy tomorrow.
In a few years, it's being predicted that Canada will have to import at least 600,000 barrels of oil a day. Even at current world prices, that's over $3 billion a year.
That's a $3 billion a year drain on our foreign currency reserves. That's $3 billion a year of inflationary pressure on our economy. That's nearly half the gross domestic product of the province of Saskatchewan. Three billion dollars a year and going up!
And yet there are people who say that governments should not build new energy projects now because they're afraid of inflation!
There are people who say that governments should not build new energy projects now because they do not understand the importance of access to these gas reserves to Canada in the pursuit of the goal of energy self-reliance and improving our balance of payments, particularly in financing the cost of the Quebec-Maritimes pipeline. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and all the premiers suggested that an application ought to go before the National Energy Board as soon as possible to test the viability of that particular project.
I will not take very much time of the House to respond to the shop-worn argument of the NDP members with regard to the establishment of some kind of guarantees of high Canadian content. We did not insist on guarantees in our agreement with the United States for a number of reasons. First, they were not necessary. We are content today that Canadian industry is

fully competitive, that it will be able to gain this business without legislated guarantees.
Next week the bill will be before the committee. Members of the New Democratic Party will be able to question the sponsors of the project. They will be able to ask them where they intend to buy their materials and whether they believe they can achieve the goal of nearly 90 per cent Canadian content. Up to the present time, Foothills have assured the National Energy Board, members of this party and me as minister that they intend to buy Canadian materials. They intend to buy Canadian steel and pipe, not Japanese pipe. Hon. members can ask the companies what they intend to do.
More than that, there is a provision in the bill by which the procurement plan listing the sources from which the company proposes to purchase its equipment, goods and materials must be submitted to the agency and the minister. If it is not satisfactory, it can be rejected by the agency and the minister. That is what is meant by effective control over Canadian content.
With regard to the suggestion that we have no ability to deal with unfair competition or dumping of foreign material, there is a provision in the bill which enables the minister to send back to the company any proposal or bid about which there is suspicion of unfair competition or dumping on the Canadian market.
In my opening speech, I argued that it is quite impossible for Canada to have these guarantees written into an international agreement without violating the provisions of our commitment under the General Agreement on Trade Tariffs. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands did not accept that argument. He is quite incorrect in suggesting that Canada and the United States are perfectly free under GATT to enter into an agreement which discriminates against other members by providing a guarantee of Canadian content. The non-discriminatory provisions of GATT do not apply to procurement by governments for their own purposes, but they certainly apply in the case of a pipeline project which is to be carried out by a private company for private purposes.
For many months we have heard suggestions from the New Democratic Party that the Americans were pressing for the adoption of a 48-inch high-pressure system from Whitehorse to Caroline in an effort to squeeze out potential Canadian suppliers. That charge was always quite untrue, but what is the response of the New Democratic Party now that we have indicated our intention to adopt a 56-inch pipe which no U.S. company is capable at present of producing? The argument advanced by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands is that Canada had been outmanoeuvred by the United States, and the United States had garnered unto itself all of the pipe business. Lo and behold, when it was announced that the pipe selected was not even manufactured in the United States, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby suddenly changed the basis of his argument and said: "I have been talking to members of the steel industry and they tell me they are not really concerned about American competition, they are now concerned about Japanese competition." Of course, the
February 23, 1978

implication of that argument is that the United States and Canada have so outmanoeuvred each other that they have handed over all the business to Japan.

I once again remind them of the benefits to Canada that are contained in this agreement with the United States and in the legislation that is before the House. The New Democratic Party intend to vote against this

legislation because they say there are no guarantees for Canadian jobs. If their will prevailed the legislation would be defeated and Canadian business would have no opportunity to compete. subtopic: CANADIAN CULTURE-FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO CULTURAL ORGANIZATIONS
CANADIAN CULTURE-FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO CULTURAL ORGANIZATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as hon. members will recall, as a result of meetings which took place on Tuesday of this week between the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) and representatives of the Professional Association of Canadian Theatres, yesterday I attempted to find out from the Secretary of State what action he had taken, particularly because of the very strongly worded press release and comments put forward by members of that association as a result of their meetings with the Secretary of State indicating the very serious situation in which a number of professional theatre groups in this country find themselves because of funding policies emanating from that department.
Members will know that over the past 20 years we have seen a tremendous expansion of professional theatre activities in this country. It is difficult to believe now that back in 1957
February 23, 1978

there were only three professional theatre companies in Canada. In the last 20 years we have seen an expansion in the number of professional theatre groups to some 133.
As hon. members know, a good deal of the incentive and encouragement for this has come from governments represented by parties on both sides of this House through regular grants put forward basically through the Canada Council. However, in recent years we have seen a situation in which the government has virtually frozen its funding.
I think it is unfortunate that the Secretary of State, in answering questions yesterday, left the clear impression that there was no real freezing of the funds of these professional theatre groups. To allow that kind of misunderstanding to stand on the record does not do him credit and certainly does not clarify the very serious situation which exists in respect of professional theatre groups. As they themselves have said, in spite of ticket price increases on the part of more than two-thirds of their members, they have been faced with a situation in which some 55 per cent have had to lay off staff, 74 per cent have virtually had to reduce the number of actors employed, and 55 per cent have incurred a greatly increased deficit. As the representatives of the Professional Association of Canadian Theatres remarked, their situation is intolerable.
The situation is well underlined in the tabling of estimates which took place yesterday. The over-all estimate of government expenditures is up by 9.3 or 9.8 per cent, depending on which figures are used. That is close in line with the average cost in the consumer price index, which is up 9.5 per cent. Even the estimates of the Secretary of State have shown a whopping increase. It runs into hundreds of millions of dollars, or approximately 25 per cent. If one looks specifically at the grants for arts and culture, one discovers the main estimates are down some 21.6 per cent. This indicates a very serious lack of commitment and concern on the part of the Secretary of State for professional theatre groups in this country.
Obviously thousands of people are now making their livelihood in professional theatre activities from coast to coast. At a time of rising unemployment and at a time when it is increasingly difficult to give people encouragement so that they can expect to have what is rightfully theirs-a job with a meaningful income-it is simply shocking that in this area of government responsibility there is no action and a declining commitment. Not only is there a freezing of the budget, there is a reducing of the federal budget in relation to this important segment of cultural activity in Canada.
Another thing which is of perhaps even greater concern is the impact that short-ranged and insufficient support lends to the importance of the cultural fabric of this country. Much has been written and many speeches have been given about the importance of maintaining national unity. The Secretary of State should know how important his role must be in maintaining the fabric of national unity.
A few weeks ago I was in Calgary. I was amazed to see the amount of professional theatre activity which has mushroomed
Adjournment Debate
in that city. I met a number of groups there, as well as a number of groups from across the country. I know the meaningful contribution these groups make toward national unity and identity. For the government to play fast and loose with cultural activity, which has increased over the last 20 years, is sheer irresponsibility.
I trust the parliamentary secretary who will be responding tonight will provide some measure of encouragement. In the three meetings which have occurred, and in the letter of the minister to the president of the Professional Association of Canadian Theatres, which was sent approximately two months late, there was no encouragement whatsoever. That is simply not a sufficient answer, in light of the serious plight of the Professional Association of Canadian Theatres.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Daudlin (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CANADIAN CULTURE-FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO CULTURAL ORGANIZATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) for his question. He will be pleased to know that today the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) received the first instalment on the 100,000 cards urging greater government support, as promised by the Professional Association of Canadian Theatres. The minister looks forward to a continued flood of mail and a continued expression of public interest in and support for our theatre in Canada.
In response to the question posed by the hon. member, I should like to quote from the minister's letter sent to Dr. Gregory Poggi, the chairman of the Professional Association of Canadian Theatres, Pact. The letter answers directly the concerns of Pact and those concerns expressed by the hon. member. It reads as follows:
I need no convincing on the subject of more public support for our artistic and cultural life: all the performing arts, including theatre, together with our visual artists, writers, filmmakers and cultural institutions such as museums, galleries, libraries, deserve and need greater financial support from the public they serve. As Secretary of State I am acutely aware that Canada's cultural growth- particularly in the realm of the arts-has long depended on the federal government's support and that of its cultural agencies such as the Canada Council, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, Canadian Film Development Corporation, National Film Board, and National Arts Centre. In recent years, support from other levels of government, from the private sector and from the public directly through audiences has broadened the financial base of the arts.
The letter goes on to state:
The $13.6 million increase in federal cultural spending that I announced last September is concrete proof of the government's commitment to Canada's cultural and artistic growth. Not only do these new funds permit us to give more support through some programs whose value to Canadian arts and culture is well recognized. Perhaps more significantly, the funds are contributing in a variety of new areas hitherto unsupported.
The 1977-78 increase in the Canada Council's budget... has meant that the council has had in many instances to keep grants at 1976-77 levels and to forgo this year making the first sustaining grants to newer companies. That in turn has forced many theatre and dance companies and orchestras to hold back on plans to more ambitious productions and schedules, or to seek more vigorously alternative sources of financing: private sector contributions, expanded subscription drives, for example. But I think it is unfair to say that because the government has, on the one hand, limited the over-all growth of an agency's budget and, on the other, provided new funds for specific areas of its total cultural program, it is taking from Peter to give to Paul.

February 23, 1978
Adjournment Debate
I would like to emphasize further that the $13.6 million that the Secretary of State announced last September was new money for ongoing and new programs across the spectrum of federal cultural activities. Theatres do benefit! Here is the specific allocation in this area: The National Theatre School received $525,000 in capital grants in 1977-78 and 1978-79. The total over four years is $2.1 million. The Canada Council touring office, received $765,000 in 1977-78 and $1,065 million in 1978-79 for increased tours, workshops for impressarios and tour organizers.
The theatre, music and dance sections received $400,000 in both 1977-78 and 1978-79 for national cultural events involving participation of performing artists and arts companies, and for master classes enabling students to work with professionals. The National Arts Centre received $150,000 in 1977-78 and $1 million in 1978-79 to establish a theatre company, consisting of two small nuclear groups, one English and the other French, for creation and touring of theatrical productions.
I trust that the information from the minister's letter to the chairman of Pact, and this added information on the allocation of some of the $13.6 million, conveys to the hon. member for Egmont the commitment of the Secretary of State and that of the government to promoting professional theatre in Canada.

subtopic: FRESHWATER FISH MARKETING CORPORATION-REASON FOR DELAY OF FINAL PAYMENT TO FISHERMEN
FRESHWATER FISH MARKETING CORPORATION-REASON FOR DELAY OF FINAL PAYMENT TO FISHERMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Manitoba produces 51 per cent of the fish that is handled by the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation located in Transcona, Manitoba. Due to the revelations that we have seen in the press in the last month and a half, I would say that the reputation of northern Manitoba fishermen is certainly in jeopardy.
At a meeting of the Northern Manitoba Commercial Fishermen's Association held on November 22 and 23, 1977, the chairman of the corporation, Mr. Peter Moss, said at that time that the fishermen would be receiving their final payment, which is due about the first part of December, in a couple of weeks. However, shortly after December 1, the chairman of the FFMC announced that no final payment would be made at that time. What has taken place since that time has certainly disheartened fishermen in Manitoba and, I am sure, has put what was once a very viable fishery into a precarious situation.
What had led to this situation is the fact that the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation has in its inventory some 14 million to 15 million pounds of fish which were purchased by the corporation. Of course, we read in the paper that much of this fish, due to freezer burn and to being stored for long periods of time, must now be dumped.
On November 22 and 23 at the meeting of the Northern Manitoba Fishermen's Association the chairman of the association, in reply to fishermen's questions, said he is getting sick and tired of people running down an efficient, well running corporation. "What are we fighting about", he asked. "We are trying to peddle your fish", he said. "We must work together closely". He suggested that they look at the beef producers

and grain growers and count their blessings. Two short weeks after that the chairman said there was no final payment for the fishermen.
In 1969 the corporation was established, and its mandate was to market fish. Since that time the corporation has been getting into other aspects of the fishing business. I suggest that the corporation has spoiled the reputation of Canadian fishermen. The quality of fish has deteriorated. It will take a long time to re-establish fish markets.
Another point is that the ability of salesmen to sell fish harvested by fishermen has diminished. It has been suggested by the Northern Manitoba Fishermen's Association that these salesmen be put on commission instead of salary.
On the editorial page of the Winnipeg Free Press for February 18 we find an article entitled "Freshwatergate?" That pertains to some very serious allegations concerning the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation. The agency has been accused of changing package dates as well as stamps.
Another article is entitled "Rabbi's OK was forged". That article accuses the corporation of changing dates on fish which had been stamped for gefilte fish and so forth.
There have been other allegations. It has been alleged that fillets have been shipped to a city dump for burning because they had been shipped to New York and some 30,000 to
40,000	pounds had been rejected by inspectors due to freezer burn. It has been alleged that trout has been kept in cold storage for far too long, and that freezer burn had to be trimmed off. It has been alleged that dates on packaging have been changed to make it appear as though the fish was fresh.
The fishermen of northern Manitoba who must try to harvest fish and get it to market in a fresh condition are losing everything they put into their operations. Technically the fish still belongs to the fishermen. They have not received their final payments, even though a partial payment has now been made. This is very discouraging for commercial fishermen.
I would like to see an immediate investigation conducted into the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation. We have dealt with the chairman of the corporation many times in the committee. The chairman has been giving the committee a whitewash job. He has also been giving fishermen's associations whitewash jobs. He just cannot seem to understand that fishermen are concerned about putting a quality product on the market for human consumption. Fishermen do not want their products stored for long periods of time. There is an allegation that fish is being dumped under the direction of management. Fishermen are complaining about that and wondering why the price of their product cannot be reduced and sold rather than dumping the product. There has been an allegation that tons of fish have been left in the open and allowed to spoil. I ask that an investigation into the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation of Manitoba be started immediately.
February 23, 1978

speakeroldname: Mr. Hugh A. Anderson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment
subtopic: FRESHWATER FISH MARKETING CORPORATION-REASON FOR DELAY OF FINAL PAYMENT TO FISHERMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation has ten members. The hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Smith) talks about irregularities and deviations from good corporate policy. I would remind the hon. member that four of those directors are active fishermen in the province of Manitoba. Although it is a Crown corporation the hon. member should realize when he makes remarks regarding the corporation in the province of Manitoba that he is not only hurting it but also the fishermen who play a very active role in the organization. I suppose I could say that the corporation has had a success which has led to some problems within the board.
The Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation, as at April 30, 1977, completed the highest sales records and profits ever.

speechtext: And the fish are still in storage.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment
subtopic: FRESHWATER FISH MARKETING CORPORATION-REASON FOR DELAY OF FINAL PAYMENT TO FISHERMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened to the hon. member and I hope he will allow me the same consideration.
Prices this past summer were increased and landings were up considerably for the summer fishing season. As a result this
Adjournment Debate
attracted fishermen who delivered greater volumes and substantially increased their earnings. Consequently, the corporation found itself at its borrowing ceiling and the board of directors made the decision to defer final payments until the cash flow improved.
On January 25, 1978, the corporation's board authorized the payment to the fishermen of 50 per cent of the final payment to be made February 24. The remainder will be paid as the cost flow situation continues to improve. In addition, the corporation is currently seeking inventory financing from the federal fisheries prices support board. This request is presently under consideration. This initiative will provide assistance until markets improve.
The Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation also provides financial assistance to fishermen to cover start-up costs when necessary. This program is well known to fishermen and is designed to assist them. Fishermen, therefore, have every reason to continue to fish this winter as they have in the past.
